title: Explaining It Broke It. What Teaching a Skill Exposed About My Understanding
body: I offered to teach a friend the accordion part I had played for two years, and within four minutes of the first lesson I discovered that I did not know how the instrument worked. I knew how to work it. The difference between those two sentences is the entire story of what teaching did to me. It started smoothly. Bellows, I said, are the breathing. Fine. Then she asked the question that broke it. Why does pushing and pulling make different sounds on the same buttons. And I stood there holding my own understanding up to the light and finding it was a lamp with no bulb. The true answer involves reed behavior and pressure and I did not have it. I had a motor memory wearing a theory's clothes. That is the first thing teaching exposes. The difference between knowing how and knowing why. Two years of playing had installed a working pilot in my hands and no engineer in my head. The gap had never mattered before, because the pilot flies and the audience claps. A student's why lands directly in the gap, every time, like water finding the crack. So I did what any honest person does. I said I did not know, and I found out, and the finding out took an evening and rearranged my playing. You cannot teach a thing without either discovering you have been driving in the fog or turning on the lights, and the lights, once on, stay on for the driver too. My bellows control improved within a week, at two years into the instrument, because I finally understood the mechanism my hands had been guessing at. The second exposure was the sequence illusion. When I played, the steps felt like a line. When I taught, the line shattered into a tree. There are three things you must understand before the fourth makes sense, two of which I had absorbed simultaneously without noticing I was absorbing a bundle. The student needed the bundle unpacked, in order, and my fluent line had no order in it at all. Fluency, it turns out, is an excellent compressor and a terrible curriculum. The third exposure was the invisible inventory. Every skill carries a basement of sub-skills the owner forgot they ever learned separately. Reading two clefs. Counting while doing something else. Tolerating the sound of a wrong note without flinching. I used all of them daily and listed none of them, until the student hit each one like an unmarked step in the dark. Teaching forced a full audit. What do I actually do when I do this. The audit's list was three times longer than my lesson plan, and the lesson plan was rewritten around the basement instead of the showroom. There is a failure mode to warn about, and I met it in the mirror. The expert trap. The temptation, when a student struggles, is to repeat the instruction louder, as if volume were the missing ingredient. The student does not need the sentence again. The student needs the prerequisite she does not have, and finding that prerequisite is the teacher's actual job. Louder is what you do instead of thinking. I said louder twice before I caught it. She can play the part now, slowly, with the pauses where the tree branches. And my own playing has a depth it did not have before her, because every explanation I prepared for her was a lesson I was secretly giving myself. Teaching, I have concluded, is the only mirror that shows the inside. You want to know what you know. Try to hand it to someone standing on the other side of your own assumptions, and watch what falls through the cracks on the way across. Then pick it up. That is your curriculum now.
